articles.title: The Man Who Ran Infosys Now Wants AI to Replace the Work That Built It
articles.excerpt: Vishal Sikka's new Palo Alto startup, Hang Ten, raised $32 million to deliver enterprise software with AI agents instead of armies of engineers — the exact model that employs hundreds of thousands of Indians.
articles.image_caption: Vishal Sikka, former Infosys CEO and founder of Hang Ten Systems, speaking at a SAP event.
articles.nri_angle: Hang Ten's AI-native delivery model directly threatens the IT-services jobs that built the Indian diaspora's H-1B pipeline — yet it is led by an Indian-origin ex-Infosys CEO and backed by Indian-American capital.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Government Is About to Become a Shareholder in Its Favorite AI Startup. The Bill Comes in GPUs.
articles.excerpt: New Delhi will take a 1-2% stake in unicorn Sarvam AI in exchange for the compute it lent under the IndiaAI Mission — a sovereign-AI experiment NRI investors and engineers should watch closely.
articles.image_caption: Ashwini Vaishnaw, India's electronics and IT minister, who oversees the IndiaAI Mission.
articles.nri_angle: India is building an AI stack it intends to own outright — models, compute and now equity — reshaping how NRI investors price Indian AI exposure and giving diaspora engineers a credible reason to build the national model back home.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Adobe's Outgoing Indian-Born CEO Is Spending His Last Act Buying AI
articles.excerpt: Shantanu Narayen's Adobe snapped up Topaz Labs and launched Firefly Foundry, doubling down on AI even as the boss who built the company prepares to hand it over.
articles.image_caption: Shantanu Narayen, chief executive of Adobe, who is steering the company through its AI transition before stepping down.
articles.nri_angle: A CEO succession at one of the few Adobe-scale companies run by an Indian-origin chief is a leadership story the diaspora tracks — and Topaz's on-device enhancement tools land squarely with NRI photographers, filmmakers and creators restoring footage across two continents.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: OpenAI Built Its Own AI Chip and Called It Jalapeño. The Real Target Is Nvidia's Fattest Margin.
articles.excerpt: Designed with Broadcom and fabbed at TSMC, the inference chip promises 50% cheaper compute — and a quiet escape from the GPU that made every Indian AI engineer's resume valuable.
articles.image_caption: OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman; the company has designed its own inference chip, codenamed Jalapeño.
articles.nri_angle: Indian engineers staff the inference, infra, and silicon teams at OpenAI, Broadcom, and TSMC's US operations — and a shift from buying Nvidia GPUs to designing custom chips reshapes which skills get hired and which get commoditized.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Wipro Just Posted $10.5 Billion in Revenue and Spun Up an 'AI-Native' Unit. The Subtext Is About Who It Stops Hiring.
articles.excerpt: Stable margins, a new forward-deployed engineering arm, and small language models for clients — Wipro's FY26 results map the exact direction India's IT giants are pulling the diaspora's careers.
articles.image_caption: A gate entrance at Wipro's Electronic City campus in Bengaluru.
articles.nri_angle: Hundreds of thousands of Indian engineers — many on H-1B and L-1 visas at Wipro's US client sites — are watching whether 'AI-native' delivery means a promotion path or a pink slip as the services model gets rebuilt around agents.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Meta Just Made a CRED Founder the Boss of WhatsApp. The Real Prize Is the 500 Million Indians Who Already Live There.
articles.excerpt: Kunal Shah, who built CRED into India's slickest fintech, takes over the world's biggest messaging app alongside Meta's $900 million bet on his company. The job is to finally make WhatsApp pay — and India is the test lab.
articles.image_caption: CRED founder Kunal Shah, named global head of WhatsApp. The real prize is the 500 million Indians already on the app (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Most NRIs run their entire Indian lives through WhatsApp — family groups, the neighbourhood kirana, airline alerts — so a payments-and-commerce overhaul led by a founder who understands Indian consumer behaviour will reshape how the diaspora moves money and shops across borders.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Hackers Dumped 630GB From the Factory That Builds a Third of India's iPhones. Apple and Tesla's Secrets Were Inside.
articles.excerpt: Tata Electronics confirmed a ransomware breach after the group World Leaks posted more than 200,000 stolen files — including documents marked as Apple and Tesla trade secrets — on the dark web.
articles.image_caption: An iPhone assembly line run by Tata Electronics in India. Hackers leaked 630GB from a plant that builds a third of India's iPhones (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: India's pitch to the diaspora and the world is that it can be a trusted alternative to China for building Apple iPhones and Tesla parts — and a 630GB leak of client trade secrets from Tata's flagship plant strikes directly at that promise, with the careers and reputations of Indian engineers riding on it.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's First Big Chip Plant Promises 48 Million Units Out of Assam by November. The Map Just Moved East.
articles.excerpt: Tata Semiconductor's packaging facility in Guwahati is on track to begin exports this year, a tangible milestone for the India Semiconductor Mission as TSMC publicly backs the country's ambitions at a Bengaluru summit.
articles.image_caption: Inside a semiconductor fabrication plant. India's first big chip facility in Assam promises 48 million units by November (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin semiconductor professionals across the Bay Area and Austin have spent years asking whether India's chip mission would ever ship a real product — and the first commercial output from an Assam plant turns a slogan into a supply chain they may one day return to or invest in.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Akash Ambani Wants to Put 1,600 Satellites Over India. He's Picking a Fight With Starlink in Orbit.
articles.excerpt: At the Reliance AGM, Jio unveiled plans for a homegrown low-earth-orbit constellation and a $10-15 billion bet to keep India's broadband sovereign. For NRIs, it is a wager on who controls the sky over the homeland.
articles.image_caption: A train of Starlink satellites photographed in low-earth orbit from a Chilean observatory
articles.nri_angle: The race to wire India from orbit decides whether the diaspora's family villages get fast broadband from an Indian operator or a foreign one, and whether a future Jio satellite IPO becomes the next big NRI investment story.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Satya Nadella's Xbox Just Got $150 Pricier and Game Pass Jumped 50%. Blame the Same Chip Crunch Hitting Everyone.
articles.excerpt: Microsoft hiked console and subscription prices overnight, citing memory costs set to double again by 2027. For the diaspora's large gaming community, the cost of play is now an AI-economy story.
articles.image_caption: The Xbox Series X and the smaller Series S console, both hit by Microsoft's price increases
articles.nri_angle: Xbox and Game Pass are staples in Indian American households where gaming bridges generations and continents, so a steep US price hike reshapes family budgets — even as the squeeze enriches the Indian-led memory supplier on the other side of the trade.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: OpenAI May Wait Until 2027 to Go Public — Because Sam Altman Wants a $1 Trillion Price Tag.
articles.excerpt: A reported IPO delay sent AI stocks reeling from Seoul to New York, tripping a KOSPI circuit breaker. For the diaspora's army of AI engineers and investors, the timing of the decade's biggest listing just got murkier.
articles.image_caption: OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, whose IPO timing is rattling global AI markets
articles.nri_angle: Indians fill the research benches at OpenAI and its rivals and tilt their portfolios toward the AI trade, so when the sector's defining IPO slips and a global selloff follows, both diaspora careers and diaspora savings feel the tremor.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Nikesh Arora Held 800 Sales Meetings in 12 Weeks. The AI Cyberthreat He's Selling Against Is Bigger Than His Stock.
articles.excerpt: Palo Alto Networks just posted 31% revenue growth and record demand as enterprises scramble to defend AI systems. For the diaspora's huge security workforce, it is the rare tech segment still hiring into the AI wave.
articles.image_caption: Palo Alto Networks chairman and CEO Nikesh Arora speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt
articles.nri_angle: Cybersecurity is the rare corner of US tech still expanding headcount through the AI shakeout, and it sits under one of the highest-paid Indian-origin CEOs in the Valley — a real signal for diaspora engineers weighing where their skills stay durable.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Apple Just Raised MacBook Prices and Blamed a Memory Shortage. The Diaspora's Next India Trip Just Got More Useful.
articles.excerpt: A chip-memory squeeze dubbed 'RAMageddon' pushed Apple to lift iPad and Mac prices for the first time mid-cycle, wiping $250 billion off its value. The same crunch is minting record profits at Indian-led Micron.
articles.image_caption: Apple raised MacBook prices, citing a memory shortage (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Higher US device prices change the household math for NRIs who already shuttle gadgets between India and America, while the memory shortage driving them is fattening the profits of Indian-led Micron and its planned Gujarat fab.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Processed 23 Billion Digital Payments in a Single Month. The Number Should Worry Visa and Mastercard.
articles.excerpt: UPI handled Rs 29.9 lakh crore in May alone, up nearly 19% in a year, as PhonePe holds 46% of the market. For NRIs, the rails they use to send money home are quietly becoming a global export.
articles.image_caption: India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) processed 23 billion transactions in a single month (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: UPI is the plumbing NRIs increasingly use to pay, split bills and send money across the India-US corridor, and its international push means the diaspora may soon scan the same QR codes abroad that they use back home.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Trump Called IBM's Indian-Born CEO a 'Legend.' Now He's Handed Arvind Krishna's Quantum Bet a Federal Tailwind.
articles.excerpt: Two new White House executive orders fast-track a working quantum computer by 2028 and post-quantum encryption by 2031 — and IBM, run by a Chennai-trained engineer, is the named beneficiary.
articles.image_caption: IBM chief executive Arvind Krishna speaking at SXSW in 2025
articles.nri_angle: An IIT Kanpur graduate now runs the company Washington is leaning on to win the quantum race — a milestone for Indian-American engineers and a signal to NRIs holding IBM stock or eyeing quantum careers.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Micron Just Told Wall Street the Memory Shortage Runs Past 2027. For the Diaspora, That's a Bill Coming Due.
articles.excerpt: Sanjay Mehrotra's company posted a blowout quarter and locked in $22 billion of advance customer commitments — but the same AI hunger that minted the gains is about to make laptops and phones pricier.
articles.image_caption: Micron Technology chief executive Sanjay Mehrotra
articles.nri_angle: An Indian-born CEO is riding the AI memory boom to record results, but the resulting chip shortage will quietly raise the cost of the laptops, phones and PC upgrades NRI families buy on both sides of the world.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A $7 Billion Chip Deal Just Bet That AI's Next Battleground Isn't the Data Center. It's the Light Switch.
articles.excerpt: Onsemi's all-stock takeover of Synaptics pushes the chip industry toward 'physical AI' — and lands squarely on the edge-computing skills a generation of Indian engineers has been building.
articles.image_caption: Close-up of a semiconductor chip on a circuit board
articles.nri_angle: The pivot from cloud AI to 'edge' AI in everyday devices reshapes where chip jobs and skills will be valuable — a direct read for Indian engineers and NRI investors tracking the semiconductor sector beyond Nvidia.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An Indian Air Force Pilot Just Became the First ISRO Astronaut on the Space Station. The Next Stop Is India's Own.
articles.excerpt: Shubhanshu Shukla's two weeks aboard the ISS are a dress rehearsal for Gaganyaan — and a recruiting poster for a space program the diaspora keeps funding from abroad.
articles.image_caption: Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla, the first ISRO astronaut to reach the International Space Station, in his Indian Air Force uniform.
articles.nri_angle: For an Indian family in New Jersey or the Bay Area, Shukla is the first of their own to fly to the space station — and the human face of a Gaganyaan program that diaspora engineers and donors have quietly been bankrolling.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: IndiaMART Connects 600 Buyers a Minute. Now It's Doubling Its AI Spend Every Six Months to Stop the Fakes.
articles.excerpt: India's biggest B2B marketplace is pouring money into AI to police counterfeit listings and replace call-centre work — a quiet test of whether Indian platforms can clean themselves up before regulators do it for them.
articles.image_caption: IndiaMART, India's largest B2B online marketplace, is doubling its AI spend to combat fraudulent listings (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: NRIs who source products from India for US storefronts — or who hold IndiaMART in their India portfolios — have a direct stake in whether the platform can scrub counterfeit and proxy sellers off a US 'Notorious Markets' watchlist.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Wants Its AI to Run on Indian Soil. A Navi Mumbai Company Is Stacking 80,000 GPUs to Make That Real.
articles.excerpt: Yotta's bet on 'sovereign' data centres — Blackwell chips, Indian data residency, no dependence on US hyperscalers — is the picks-and-shovels play behind India's AI ambitions. The diaspora's startups are the customers.
articles.image_caption: Rows of servers in a data centre; Yotta is stacking 80,000 GPUs to build sovereign AI infrastructure in Navi Mumbai
articles.nri_angle: Indian AI startups founded by returnees and NRIs need compute that keeps data inside India for regulatory and cost reasons — Yotta's GPU farms are the rails those companies, and diaspora investors backing them, are betting on.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Microsoft Bankrolled the AI Giants. Now Satya Nadella Is Picking a Fight With Them.
articles.excerpt: The Hyderabad-born CEO warns AI can't 'hollow out' white-collar work — the work his own Indian engineers do most — while a model-agnostic Copilot quietly reshapes the race.
articles.image_caption: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, who has called for an AI 'reset' away from a few dominant model makers.
articles.nri_angle: Nadella's warning against AI 'hollowing out' white-collar jobs lands directly on the young Indian engineers — in Hyderabad, Bengaluru and on H-1B visas in the US — whose entry-level coding roles are most exposed, and a commodity-AI world gives India's services giants room to survive.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Everyone's Chasing AI Chips. An Indian-American Duo Just Raised $190 Million Building the Wires Between Them.
articles.excerpt: Upscale AI hit a $2 billion valuation with Nvidia and Azim Premji's fund backing it — and its founders' résumés read like a tour of Silicon Valley's Indian engineering diaspora.
articles.image_caption: High-speed networking between AI servers — the bottleneck Upscale AI's silicon targets, backed by a 90 million raise
articles.nri_angle: While layoff headlines hit Indian software engineers, the AI infrastructure layer — led by diaspora veterans like Upscale's Barun Kar and Rajiv Khemani and Arista's Jayshree Ullal — is hiring and offers NRI engineers and investors a more defensible bet than the model labs.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Firm That Spotted Zomato Early Just Put Half Its Money Into AI and Deeptech
articles.excerpt: Info Edge has quietly poured ₹1,003 crore into 54 AI and deeptech startups — and for NRI investors it's a rare public-market window into India's next tech decade.
articles.image_caption: Info Edge, the Naukri.com parent that backed Zomato early, is putting half its investments into AI and deeptech (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Info Edge is among the most-watched listed proxies for India's startup economy, giving NRI investors early, diversified exposure to AI and deeptech they otherwise can't reach — and the ventures it funds are exactly the kind that make a return-to-India career move credible.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Won't Ban Crypto. It Just Made Sure It Can See Every Trade Over $10,000.
articles.excerpt: A new reporting order for over-the-counter deals, plus fresh Travel Rule pop-ups on Binance, signal the government's real crypto policy: tolerate it, tax it, and trace it.
articles.image_caption: Cryptocurrency; India will monitor large crypto trades rather than ban them
articles.nri_angle: NRIs who move money between Indian and US wallets, or hold Indian-exchange accounts from abroad, now face name-and-PAN disclosure on transfers — a compliance headache that turns cross-border crypto into a paper trail.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Qualcomm Spent 25 Years Selling Phone Chips. It Just Told Wall Street Two-Thirds of Its Future Isn't Phones.
articles.excerpt: An Investor Day blitz — a $40 billion non-handset target, Meta and Microsoft as data-center customers, and a $3.9 billion software buy — repositions the company as an AI infrastructure player. The talent it needs is heavily Indian.
articles.image_caption: Qualcomm; the chipmaker says most of its future revenue will come from outside smartphones
articles.nri_angle: Qualcomm's pivot into AI data-center chips is a hiring story as much as a strategy story — it opens a new front in the Silicon Valley engineering job market just as legacy IT firms shed roles, and Indian chip-design talent sits at the center of it.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Anthropic and Amazon Just Picked 40 Indian Startups to Build the Next Wave of AI Agents. The Catch: No Equity, Big Strings.
articles.excerpt: An India-first accelerator hands early-stage founders Claude access and $70,000 in credits. It is also a quiet land-grab for the developer loyalty that will decide who owns India's AI stack.
articles.image_caption: A tech park in Bengaluru; Anthropic and AWS selected 40 Indian startups to build agentic-AI products
articles.nri_angle: For NRI founders and angel investors, this is the clearest signal yet that the agentic-AI startup action is moving to Bengaluru — and that US frontier labs, not just US capital, now compete directly for India's best builders.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Accenture Beat on Profit and Still Fell 7%. The Reason Is the One Job Indians Do Most for It.
articles.excerpt: The consulting giant's revenue missed and it trimmed its full-year outlook — as the same AI it is selling clients starts eating the advisory work that built its India headcount.
articles.image_caption: Accenture's office building in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, one of its largest delivery hubs in India
articles.nri_angle: Accenture employs more people in India than in any other country — over 300,000 — so when its consulting demand softens and AI starts replacing advisory billable hours, the squeeze lands first on the Indian and Indian-American professionals who staff its delivery centers and US client teams.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Meta Just Made AI Glasses Cheap Enough to Go Mass-Market. The First Test Will Be the Indian Diaspora's Wishlist.
articles.excerpt: At $299 and running Meta's first in-house Superintelligence model, the new Meta Glasses drop the price barrier — and put a camera-and-AI face computer within reach of the NRI early adopter.
articles.image_caption: Meta's Ray-Ban smart glasses with charging case, the predecessor to the new lower-cost Meta Glasses line
articles.nri_angle: Indian-Americans are among the heaviest early adopters of AI gadgets and the most frequent international travelers and video-callers home — exactly the use cases (live translation, hands-free capture) Meta is selling — making the diaspora a natural first market for a sub-$300 AI wearable.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Wall Street Bank Just Told India Its AI Is a 'Fighter Jet' It Doesn't Own. The Warning Is a Gift to the Diaspora's Startups.
articles.excerpt: Bernstein says India risks running its banks, defense and government on foreign AI models that could be switched off in a crisis — and the case for homegrown 'sovereign AI' has never paid off faster for founders like Sarvam.
articles.image_caption: AI computing infrastructure; a Wall Street bank warns India does not own its core AI capability
articles.nri_angle: The sovereign-AI push is creating a new class of Indian deep-tech companies — many founded or funded by returning diaspora technologists — and the geopolitical risk Bernstein flags (foreign AI access cut overnight) is precisely the same export-control logic the US just used against Anthropic, making this a live investment and career thesis for NRIs in AI.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Amazon Just Added $13 Billion to Its India Bet. The Money Is Going Where the H-1B Jobs Used to Go.
articles.excerpt: A fresh AWS commitment pushes Amazon's India spend toward $75 billion by 2030 — and it lands as the company builds the AI and cloud capacity at home that once required sending engineers abroad.
articles.image_caption: An Amazon data centre; the company is pouring another $13 billion into AI and cloud in India (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: For Indian engineers weighing a US move against staying put, Amazon is quietly answering the question: the best-paid cloud and AI work is increasingly being built inside India, not just in Seattle.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Sundar Pichai's Gemini Can Now Run Your Browser, Phone, and Desktop. The Race Just Moved From Chatbots to Agents.
articles.excerpt: Google opened up Gemini 3.5 Flash to build custom agents that take actions across platforms — the clearest sign yet that the AI fight has shifted from answering questions to doing the work.
articles.image_caption: Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai
articles.nri_angle: Indian engineers building on AI — at Google, at Indian startups, or on the side — now have a cheaper agent platform to ship on, but also a sharper reason to worry about which of their own tasks the agents automate first.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's IT Giants Used to Run on H-1B Visas. New Data Shows They've Quietly Stopped Needing Them.
articles.excerpt: H-1B approvals for the top seven Indian IT firms fell 37% in a year and 70% from a decade ago, as localization, automation, and AI rewrite the offshore business model that built the industry.
articles.image_caption: An Infosys campus in India; the country's IT majors have sharply cut their reliance on H-1B visas (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: The visa pipeline that brought a generation of Indian engineers to America is narrowing not just because of Washington, but because the IT industry itself no longer needs it — a structural shift every NRI with family in the sector should understand.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Adobe's Indian-Born CEO Bet the Company on Selling Software. On His Way Out, He's Giving It Away.
articles.excerpt: Shantanu Narayen built Creative Cloud into a subscription juggernaut. His parting move — a freemium, AI-first Adobe — will define what the next Indian-American who runs it inherits.
articles.image_caption: Adobe CEO Shantanu Narayen, who announced his retirement in 2026 after nearly two decades leading the company.
articles.nri_angle: Adobe is one of the largest employers of Indian engineers and creative professionals in the Bay Area, and its succession question is a live test of whether the diaspora's grip on Silicon Valley's top jobs outlasts the executives who built it.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Apple Spent 15 Years Escaping Intel. Now It's Quietly Going Back — and the Reason Sits in a Memory-Chip Shortage.
articles.excerpt: A tentative Apple-Intel foundry deal is being sold as a US manufacturing win. For Indian engineers and NRI investors, the real signal is how fragile the chip supply chain has become.
articles.image_caption: A silicon wafer under inspection; Apple is exploring Intel's 18A-P process for lower-end Mac and iPad chips (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Indian engineers staff the chip-design and supply-chain teams at Apple, Intel, TSMC, and Micron, and India's own fab ambitions live or die by exactly the foundry economics this deal exposes — making it required reading for NRIs in semiconductors and the investors tracking them.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ola Electric Once Owned Half of India's Electric Scooter Market. The Companies That Took It Are the Boring Ones.
articles.excerpt: As India's EV two-wheeler race shifts from land-grab to profit, the quiet operators — Ather, TVS, Bajaj — are winning. For NRI investors, that change of rules is the whole story.
articles.image_caption: An Ola Electric S1 scooter; India's e-two-wheeler market is shifting from volume to profitability (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: India's listed EV makers — Ola Electric and Ather among them — are increasingly in NRI portfolios, and the sector's pivot from market-share blitz to margin discipline changes which of these stocks is actually worth owning.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Vishal Sikka Ran Infosys. Now He's Built an AI Startup Aimed at Killing the Business He Came From.
articles.excerpt: The former Infosys CEO's new venture, Hang Ten Systems, raised $32 million to let AI do the integration-and-maintenance grunt work that built India's $315 billion IT industry.
articles.image_caption: Vishal Sikka, former CEO of Infosys, speaking at an enterprise technology conference.
articles.nri_angle: Hundreds of thousands of Indian engineers — in Bengaluru delivery centers and on H-1B and L-1 visas at US client sites — earn a living doing exactly the integration and maintenance work Sikka now wants software to automate.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Washington Just Cut Off Foreign Nationals From Anthropic's Best AI. India's 'Sovereign AI' Startups Got the Gift of the Year.
articles.excerpt: A US export-control order barring all foreign nationals — even Anthropic's own employees — from its top models has made the case for homegrown AI overnight. Sarvam and a wave of Indian builders are the unexpected winners.
articles.image_caption: roger4336 via flickr (BY-SA)
articles.nri_angle: Indian engineers and founders building or relying on frontier AI just watched access to the best US model get revoked in 90 minutes — proof that for NRIs and India alike, depending on a single foreign lab is now a strategic risk, not a convenience.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's IT Giants Just Lost ₹8.5 Lakh Crore in Five Years. The Companies Replacing Them on the Value Charts Are AI Startups.
articles.excerpt: TCS, Infosys, and Wipro are the only major Indian sector to post a cumulative decline in value — while four pure-play AI firms, led by Sarvam, crashed onto the rankings. For NRI investors, the great rotation is here.
articles.image_caption: The Bombay Stock Exchange; India's listed IT majors have shed ₹8.5 lakh crore in market value over five years
articles.nri_angle: NRIs hold Indian IT through mutual funds, ADRs, and direct stakes as the safe, dividend-paying bet on India's tech story — but the value is rotating from the outsourcers their generation worked for to the AI startups disrupting them.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's First Private Rocket-to-Orbit Is on the Pad. The Company Behind It Isn't ISRO.
articles.excerpt: Skyroot's Vikram-1 is in final preparations at Sriharikota for the maiden orbital flight of an Indian private rocket — backed by GIC, BlackRock and an early Google investor.
articles.image_caption: Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-S rocket lifts off on Mission Prarambh from Sriharikota in November 2022, India's first private rocket to reach space.
articles.nri_angle: For NRI investors eyeing India's marquee IPOs and for diaspora aerospace engineers weighing a move home, Skyroot's launch is proof that India now has a private space economy — not just a state space programme.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Set Its Chip Budget for the Year: Rs 7,100 Crore, and a Quiet Bet on Design Over Fabs
articles.excerpt: The FY27 plan funds one fab, nine manufacturing units and thirty design firms — an admission that India will compete where its engineers already dominate, not where Taiwan does.
articles.image_caption: A 200mm semiconductor wafer fabrication line, the kind of back-end and manufacturing capacity India's FY27 incentives target.
articles.nri_angle: For the Indian-origin chip engineer at Nvidia or Qualcomm, India's design-led semiconductor bet is the clearest 'you could do this at home' signal yet — aimed at exactly the work the diaspora already dominates abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Oracle Just Told the SEC That AI Cost 21,000 Jobs. India Took More Than Half of Them.
articles.excerpt: The most candid admission yet that AI is replacing tech workers came in a regulatory filing — and roughly 12,000 of the cuts landed in India, where Oracle's largest workforce sits.
articles.image_caption: Oracle, which told the SEC that AI adoption contributed to cutting about 21,000 jobs (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Oracle is the first major tech firm to put AI job losses in writing to regulators, and with India absorbing the largest share, it is a warning shot for every Indian engineer on an H-1B watching the same companies spend on data centers while thinning their ranks.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Got Its First 'Sovereign AI' Unicorn. The Twist Is Who Wrote the Biggest Cheque.
articles.excerpt: Bengaluru's Sarvam AI raised $234 million at a $1.5 billion valuation — but the lead investor was not a global VC. It was HCLTech, an Indian IT giant betting $150 million on homegrown models.
articles.image_caption: HCLTech led the funding round in Sarvam AI, India's first 'sovereign AI' unicorn (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Sarvam's round is the clearest sign yet that India intends to build its own AI stack rather than rent one from Silicon Valley — a shift that reshapes where diaspora engineers and NRI investors place their bets on the next decade of Indian tech.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Nvidia Gets the Headlines. But an Indian-Origin CEO Sells the One Chip AI Data Centers Can't Run Without.
articles.excerpt: SiTime, led by Rajesh Vashist, makes the timing chips that keep AI clusters in sync. Revenue jumped 88%, the stock has roughly tripled this year, and inference may need four times more of its product.
articles.image_caption: A close-up of a motherboard and microchips, the kind of precision components SiTime designs for AI data centers
articles.nri_angle: While the diaspora obsesses over Nvidia, an Indian-origin CEO is quietly riding the same AI wave from an unglamorous corner of the chip stack — a reminder that the semiconductor boom NRI investors and engineers are tracking runs far deeper than GPUs.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Credit-Card Rewards Founder From Bengaluru Just Got Handed WhatsApp's 3 Billion Users
articles.excerpt: Meta is putting $900 million into CRED and naming Kunal Shah as WhatsApp's first Indian chief. The diaspora's most-used app now answers to a man who built his name on getting Indians to pay their bills on time.
articles.image_caption: Kunal Shah, founder of CRED and FreeCharge, now appointed global head of WhatsApp
articles.nri_angle: WhatsApp is the connective tissue of the Indian diaspora — the app NRIs use to call parents in Pune and run side businesses in New Jersey — and it will now be steered by an Indian founder whose payments instincts point the monetization experiments straight at India first.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Hackers Put Apple and Tesla Trade Secrets on the Dark Web. The Leak Came From a Tata Plant in Tamil Nadu.
articles.excerpt: A ransomware crew claims to have lifted iPhone inspection manuals and Tesla part drawings from Tata Electronics, the company carrying India's bet that it can build the West's gadgets. The breach lands as India races to become Apple's factory floor.
articles.image_caption: Tata Electronics, the Tata Group arm that assembles iPhones in India, suffered a data breach (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: The 'Made in India' iPhone in an NRI's pocket depends on Tata's Tamil Nadu plants staying secure and trusted; a breach exposing Apple and Tesla secrets is a direct test of whether India can be the world's trusted manufacturing base, not just its cheapest one.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Promised Chips for Years. By November, a Tata Plant in Assam Says It Will Actually Ship 48 Million of Them.
articles.excerpt: A state once defined by insurgency is about to become a semiconductor exporter. For a diaspora that has watched India announce fabs and miss deadlines, a concrete shipping date is the news.
articles.image_caption: Tata Semiconductor's Assam ATMP plant aims to begin exporting packaged chips by November (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Semiconductor professionals in the diaspora have heard India's chip promises before; the first real export volumes out of Assam are the proof point that decides whether 'return to India' is a serious career bet or still aspirational.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: UPI Was Built So Indians Could Split a Dinner Bill. It Just Went Live at a Paris Department Store.
articles.excerpt: India's payments rail now works in eleven countries, from the Eiffel Tower to a Cambodian street market. For the diaspora, the home-screen app is quietly becoming a passport.
articles.image_caption: A shopper makes a contactless QR-code payment with a smartphone, the everyday gesture UPI is now exporting abroad.
articles.nri_angle: NRIs who fly home no longer need to juggle forex cards or cash across nine-plus countries — the same UPI app on their phone now pays merchants from Paris to Phnom Penh, and the corridor map is expanding toward the markets where the diaspora actually lives.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An Indian-Born CEO Now Supplies the Memory for Claude — and Has Bought a Slice of the Company That Builds It.
articles.excerpt: Micron's deal with Anthropic ties Sanjay Mehrotra's memory empire directly to a frontier AI lab, days before an earnings report that could show a tenfold jump in profit.
articles.image_caption: A green memory module on a circuit board — the high-bandwidth memory at the centre of the AI build-out.
articles.nri_angle: For NRI investors holding Micron and for the thousands of Indian engineers inside the memory and AI-infrastructure supply chain, the Anthropic pact is a signal that the chip cycle that funds their RSUs has shifted from boom-and-bust to a structural AI build-out — with an Indian-American CEO sitting at the chokepoint.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Cognizant Just Wired ServiceNow's AI Agents Into Its Own. The Indian IT Workforce Is the Experiment.
articles.excerpt: An open-source 'agent orchestrator' lets one company's bots talk to another's. For the millions who staff India's services industry, it is a preview of the job that is being automated.
articles.image_caption: Cognizant Technology Solutions via flickr (BY-SA)
articles.nri_angle: Cognizant employs hundreds of thousands of Indians and is a top sponsor of H-1B workers in the US; its push to make AI agents do cross-platform enterprise work is a direct signal to NRI techies in IT services about which roles get automated first — and which become more valuable.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Wall Street Asked If Arista's AI Boom Was Over. Jayshree Ullal Just Lifted the Bet to 1.6 Terabits.
articles.excerpt: Arista Networks grew revenue 35% to $2.7 billion as hyperscalers wired their AI data centres with its switches. The Indian-origin CEO is now selling the plumbing for the next wave.
articles.image_caption: Jayshree Ullal, chairperson and CEO of Arista Networks
articles.nri_angle: Arista is one of Silicon Valley's quietest wealth machines for Indian-American engineers and investors, and its fortunes now ride entirely on whether the AI data-centre build-out keeps going.
